title: Number bonds & fact families
examples: Can you show me a fact family for the number five?
What do you mean by inverse facts?
How do I use a fact triangle?

explain.say: Today we are learning about number bonds. A number bond shows how numbers stick together to make a bigger number.
Look at this bond. Two and three are the parts. They join together to make five, which is the whole.
Next, we look at fact families. These are groups of three numbers that are related to each other.
A fact family uses addition and subtraction. For example, three plus four is seven. So, seven minus three is four.
We can also use fact triangles. The big corner number is the whole. The other two numbers are the parts.

faq.a: A number bond shows that two smaller numbers, or parts, join together to make one larger number, which is the whole.
asks: How do I see the parts and the whole?

faq.a: Inverse facts are the opposite facts. If you know that two plus three equals five, then you also know that five minus two equals three.

faq.q: How do I use a fact triangle?
faq.a: In a fact triangle, the largest number at the top is the whole. The two numbers at the bottom are the parts that make it.
asks: Is the top number always the biggest?

faq.q: Can I use number bonds for bigger numbers?
faq.a: Yes, you can use them for numbers up to twenty or even up to one hundred. The idea stays the same.

faq.q: What if I forget one part?
faq.a: If you forget a part, you can use the fact family or the triangle to help you find the missing number.
asks: What if I need to find a missing number?

facts: A number bond shows parts joining to make a whole.
Fact families use addition and subtraction together.
In a fact triangle, the top number is always the whole.
If two numbers make a total, they are a number bond pair.

quiz.say: Which set of numbers correctly shows the fact family for 5, 2, and 3?
quiz.why: This is correct because two and three are the parts that join to make the whole number five.

wrong.0: This is tempting because it uses the numbers, but it makes the wrong whole number, seven.
wrong.2: This is a correct fact, but the question asks for the set that shows the relationship, and this option only shows one subtraction fact.
wrong.3: This is incorrect because adding two and five gives you seven, not the whole number five.

quiz.say: If the parts are six and four, what is the whole number?
quiz.why: You join six and four together. When you count up, you reach ten, so ten is the whole.

wrong.0: This is too big; you are only working with the numbers six and four.
wrong.2: This is a common mistake because you might be adding the numbers together but forgetting to count back to the start.
wrong.3: This is wrong because you are subtracting the numbers instead of adding them together.

quiz.say: Look at the fact triangle. If the whole is ten and one part is seven, what is the missing part?
quiz.why: The whole is ten. If you take away seven, you are left with three. So, three is the missing part.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you added the two numbers together instead of finding the difference.
wrong.1: This is a common mistake when subtracting, but you need to count down from ten.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you used the whole number as the answer instead of finding the missing part.
